Sprigs
sprĭgz
n. pl. (small shoots or sprays put forth by a vine or tree)
Of Northern origin, akin to the Saxon sprec, a shoot. Scripture uses it twice, both times of growth that is about to be cut — the sprigs of Isaiah's vineyard taken off with pruning hooks, and the sprigs of Ezekiel's low vine.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah sets the word in a harvest that never comes: “For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches” (Isaiah 18:5). The timing is the severity. The cutting falls not on a barren plant but on one that is doing everything a plant should — budding, flowering, setting fruit — and it falls before the harvest, so that all the promise of the season is removed at the moment it is most visible. Ezekiel uses the word of a vine deliberately kept small: “And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs” (Ezekiel 17:6). It is a real vine and it really grows, but it grows toward the wrong sovereign. The Lord Jesus takes up the same husbandry and gives the rule that governs it: “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (John 15:2). And He states the end of the shoot that is merely attached: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned” (John 15:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sprig as a shoot, twig or small branch; a spray.

expand to see more

SPRIG, n. A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray.

PRUNE, v.t. To lop or cut off the superfluous branches of trees, to make them bear better fruit or grow higher.

PRUNING-HOOK, n. An instrument used in pruning trees, having a hooked or curved blade.

VINE, n. The plant which produces grapes; a climbing or trailing plant.

HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 18:5 — "For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches."

Ezekiel 17:6 — "And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs."

John 15:2 — "Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit."

John 15:6 — "If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned."

Modern Corruption

Pruning is recast as a gentle metaphor for personal growth, and the cutting off of fruitless branches is quietly dropped from the vineyard.

expand to see more

John 15 is preached constantly and halved routinely. The purging of the fruitful branch survives, softened into the reassurance that difficulty is God improving us. The first clause of the verse — every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away — is passed over, and with it the seriousness that makes the second clause a comfort rather than a platitude. Isaiah's picture is the necessary corrective: the sprigs were cut with pruning hooks before the harvest, while the bud was perfect. God's husbandry is not sentimental about promise. It is interested in fruit.

The second corruption is the confusion of attachment with abiding. Ezekiel's vine of low stature grew, spread, and shot forth sprigs; by every visible measure it was alive, and it was planted by a gardener whose purpose it served rather than God's. Our Lord draws the same distinction between the branch that is in me and bears, and the man who does not abide and is gathered for burning. The doctrine the church needs here is the one the Reformed confessions state plainly: outward membership in the visible vine is not union with Christ, and the difference between the two is not visible in the spring. It is visible at harvest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zalzallim (H2150), sprigs or tendrils; mazmeroth (H4211), pruning hooks; gephen (H1612), a vine; Greek kathairo (G2508), to cleanse or prune.

expand to see more

Hebrew zalzallim (H2150) — quivering sprigs, tendrils; Isaiah 18:5.

Hebrew mazmeroth (H4211) — pruning hooks, the vinedresser's knife.

Hebrew gephen (H1612) — a vine; Ezekiel's spreading vine of low stature.

Greek kathairo (G2508) — to cleanse, prune; John 15:2, he purgeth it.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; the condition of fruitfulness in John 15.

Usage

"“He shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks” — cutting before the harvest."

"“Shot forth sprigs” — a vine that grows toward the wrong king."

"“He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” — the husbandman's purpose."
